item.title: Q-CTRL Deploys Fire Opal Dynamics Simulator on IBM Quantum Functions, Achieving 12× Speedup on Nighthawk
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that Q‑CTRL’s Fire Opal Dynamics Simulator can now run on IBM Quantum Functions and deliver a twelve‑fold speedup on the new Nighthawk r2 processor versus the older Heron r3 hardware, a leap that makes large‑scale fermionic many‑body simulations practical for a single API call. By combining deterministic crosstalk suppression with quantum‑accelerated dynamics, the service bridges a gap between noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices and classical tensor‑network methods, opening faster pathways for computational chemistry and materials design. The result underscores how hardware‑software co‑design is becoming essential to extract real scientific value from today’s quantum processors, even as fidelity constraints still limit problem size. Readers should watch this development as a template for future cloud‑based quantum simulation platforms that promise tangible research productivity gains.

Q-CTRL has deployed its Fire Opal Dynamics Simulator on IBM Quantum Functions, achieving a 12x speedup on Nighthawk r2 processors compared to Heron r3 systems for large-scale fermionic many-body physics simulations. This allows researchers to execute complex simulations with a single API call, significantly accelerating computational chemistry and materials modeling. The Dynamics Simulator, available in the IBM Quantum Functions Catalog, employs advanced techniques like deterministic crosstalk suppression to maintain high fidelity and overcome limitations of classical tensor networks. item.title: Q-CTRL Expands Fire Opal Suite with Constrained Optimization, Estimator Twirling, and Monte Carlo Solver
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how Q‑CTRL is turning its Fire Opal platform into a more application‑ready toolbox by adding features that directly address two of the biggest bottlenecks in near‑term quantum work: algorithmic performance and hardware noise. The constrained‑optimization extension for QAOA pushes approximation ratios well beyond what vanilla implementations achieve, echoing recent research that couples problem‑specific constraints with variational circuits to squeeze extra value from noisy devices. Meanwhile, Estimator Pauli twirling promises a measurable boost in signal‑to‑noise without any extra shots—a practical win for anyone running hybrid workloads—while the Monte Carlo finance module demonstrates that even 17–27 qubit runs can be orchestrated at scale, hinting at early‑stage quantum advantage use cases. Together these upgrades illustrate a maturing ecosystem where software layers are increasingly able to compensate for hardware limitations and bring real‑world problems within reach.

Q-CTRL has updated its Fire Opal platform with new features including constrained optimization for QAOA, significantly increasing approximation ratios. They've also introduced Monte Carlo integration for quantitative finance, capable of scaling hardware execution up to 17-27 qubits. Additionally, Fire Opal now includes Estimator Pauli Twirling to improve signal-to-noise ratio with zero additional QPU shot overhead. item.title: Q-CTRL Demonstrates Push-Button Cold-Start Calibration on QuantWare Superconducting QPUs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases a practical step toward removing the labor‑intensive “tuning” phase that has long limited the throughput of superconducting processors, demonstrating that a 21‑qubit device can be taken from cold start to usable gate fidelities in under three hours without human intervention. By integrating Q‑CTRL’s Boulder Opal platform with QuantWare hardware, the work builds on recent automation efforts such as IBM’s “zero‑touch” calibration and Google’s automated error mitigation pipelines, highlighting a convergence toward fully self‑optimizing quantum stacks. If the approach scales to larger arrays, it could dramatically shorten experiment turnaround times and make cloud‑based access to high‑fidelity qubits more reliable, though its performance on devices with tighter cross‑talk constraints remains to be validated.

Q-CTRL has demonstrated an autonomous, cold-start calibration process for QuantWare superconducting processors using its Boulder Opal control platform. This technology can bring a 21-qubit QuantWare Contralto-D21 device from an uncalibrated state to operational gate fidelities in under three hours, significantly reducing the manual effort and time typically required. This innovation addresses a major bottleneck in scaling superconducting quantum computers by automating the complex tuning and stabilization of control parameters, which often fail with conventional methods due to environmental drift. item.title: IBM, Mitsubishi Chemical, and Keio Train Generative Quantum Eigensolvers on 70-Qubit Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a hybrid quantum‑classical workflow—leveraging an autoregressive transformer to train generative quantum eigensolvers directly on IBM’s 70‑qubit processor—can dramatically cut gate counts and circuit depth when modeling strongly correlated organotin photoresist molecules. By demonstrating chemistry‑relevant simulations with far fewer resources, the work builds on recent advances in variational algorithms and quantum‑machine‑learning pipelines, moving them from theory toward practical, near‑term hardware use. The collaboration between IBM, Mitsubishi Chemical, Keio University and NVIDIA also signals growing industry interest in applying quantum methods to complex materials design, though scaling beyond 70 qubits will still require further error mitigation and hardware improvements.

IBM Quantum, Mitsubishi Chemical, Keio University, and NVIDIA have successfully demonstrated a quantum hardware training framework for generative quantum eigensolvers on a 70-qubit processor. This framework, using an autoregressive transformer, was used to simulate complex organotin photoresist molecules with significantly reduced gate counts and circuit depths compared to conventional methods. The research highlights a new approach to overcoming the challenges of simulating strongly correlated electrons in organometallic clusters using quantum computing. item.title: RIKEN and Quantinuum Demonstrate Heterogeneous Multi-QPU Workflows on Fugaku
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases the first large‑scale heterogeneous quantum workflow that couples a world‑leading classical supercomputer with two fundamentally different QPUs—Quantinuum’s trapped‑ion processor and IBM’s superconducting chip—demonstrating that distinct hardware can be orchestrated to tackle a single scientific problem more efficiently. By cutting the energy error in a 16‑site 2D transverse‑field Ising model, the experiment proves that hybrid multi‑QPU pipelines can extract complementary strengths (high fidelity gates versus fast operation) and may become a practical route toward near‑term quantum advantage. The use of Tierkreis to manage distributed resources also signals a maturing software stack for cross‑platform quantum orchestration, an essential step as larger ecosystems of specialized processors emerge. Readers should note that the demonstration remains at modest qubit counts, so scaling the approach will require further advances in error mitigation and interconnect latency.

Researchers successfully demonstrated a hybrid quantum-classical computing architecture integrating the Fugaku supercomputer with two distinct quantum processors: Quantinuum's trapped-ion Reimei and IBM's superconducting ibm_kobe. This setup enabled a multi-modality workflow, significantly reducing energy error in a 16-site 2D Transverse-Field Ising Model calculation by combining the strengths of both quantum systems. The Tierkreis workflow management system was adapted to orchestrate these complex computations across geographically separated quantum processing units. item.title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first quantum‑hardware study of nonperturbative string dynamics in a genuine (2+1)‑dimensional lattice gauge theory, using 63 superconducting qubits to evolve Z₂ electric flux strings with dynamical matter and magnetic plaquette terms. By directly measuring Gauss‑law constraints and employing ancilla‑based error checks, the team pushes real‑time simulations beyond the entanglement limits of classical tensor‑network methods, opening a practical route toward exploring confinement and deconfinement in higher‑dimensional gauge models. The results signal that near‑term quantum processors are already capable of tackling problems of direct relevance to high‑energy physics, even though further improvements in coherence and error mitigation will be needed to reach larger lattices and longer evolution times.

Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.

item.title: Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a fully on‑chip dissipation scheme that can reset superconducting transmons in roughly 50 ns while keeping residual excitations below one percent, a speed and fidelity level that directly benefits the rapid measurement–feedback loops required for quantum error correction. By embedding resistive loads in dedicated resonators, the approach sidesteps thermal noise from external wiring and offers intrinsic Purcell protection, making it far more scalable than earlier reset methods that relied on bulky cryogenic attenuators or active microwave drives. If integrated into larger processors, such fast, passive reset could shrink QEC cycle times and reduce leakage‑induced logical errors without adding significant hardware overhead.

Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the $|g\rangle-|e\rangle$ transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of $0.29\%$ and $0.67\%$ for qubits initialized in $|g\rangle$ and $|e\rangle$, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the $|f\rangle$ state, reducing its residual population to $0.51\%$. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.

item.title: High-Speed Control of a Fluxonium Qubit via Picosecond Pulses from Josephson Digital Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that picosecond single‑flux‑quantum pulses from Josephson digital circuits can drive fluxonium qubits with gate fidelities exceeding 99.99 percent, overcoming the long‑standing difficulty of applying SFQ control to low‑frequency devices. By introducing a simple high‑frequency pulse‑packet scheme and a more aggressive phase‑shifted flux‑and‑charge sequence, the authors show both robust operation across parameter variations and substantially faster gates than previously possible. The work paves the way for fully cryogenic, scalable control electronics that could dramatically reduce wiring heat load and accelerate the integration of fluxonium into larger quantum processors.

We develop a control strategy for fluxonium qubits based on picosecond single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses generated by Josephson digital circuits. A major challenge is that SFQ protocols originally designed for transmon control become inefficient for low-frequency fluxonium. In this regime, the asymmetry of flux and charge couplings leads either to excessive leakage or excessively long gate times. We show that this limitation can be overcome by two complementary protocols. The first protocol employs high-frequency SFQ pulse packets applied through the flux channel, offering a simple, analytically transparent, and robust approach for high-fidelity single-qubit control. The second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and reduce the gate duration. Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above $99.99\%$; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

item.title: Reading long-range information from a separable quantum record requires entangled measurements
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a completely separable array of qubit probes can nonetheless encode long‑range spin correlations, but extracting that information reliably demands joint (entangled) measurements rather than any locally implementable strategy. By pinpointing the precise overlap window where separable readouts collapse to random guessing while entangled readouts retain a distance‑independent advantage, it clarifies an operational separation between state entanglement and measurement entanglement—a theme echoed in recent advances on distributed quantum sensing and resource theories of measurements. The result suggests that future quantum sensor networks may need collective readout hardware to unlock the full informational content of locally generated records, even when the probes themselves remain unentangled.

Qubit probes record the relative orientation of neighboring, initially uncorrelated Ising spins through local interactions. Each probe encodes one bond label in two states with overlap $1-p$. The resulting probe record is fully separable. A receiver gets one copy and guesses whether two distant spins point in the same or opposite directions. On the square lattice, the best readout with separable measurement effects approaches success probability $1/2$ as the spin separation grows, for $0<p\le p_0=1-1/\sqrt2$. This includes all local operations with classical communication. The same conclusion holds for every measurement whose effects remain positive under partial transposition across every cut of the probes. For $p_*=0.29181\le p\le1$, a joint readout of the same record maintains a success probability above $1/2$ by a positive amount independent of distance. The overlap $[p_*,p_0]$ gives a strict separation between the readouts. A record that is created locally and contains no entanglement can therefore hold long-range information that only measurements with entangled effects can read.

item.title: Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a quantum‑enhanced graph‑decomposition step can boost QAOA’s performance on hard MaxCut instances by pruning the problem before the variational run, delivering consistently higher approximation ratios than prior decomposition schemes and recent QAOA variants. By leveraging QAOA itself as a sparsification subroutine, the authors sidestep the exponential integer‑program bottleneck of earlier methods while still fitting within near‑term hardware limits. The results suggest a practical pathway to scale combinatorial optimization on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum devices, though the approach remains heuristic and its advantage on much larger or highly irregular graphs has yet to be demonstrated.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a near-term quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its accuracy and resource requirements may scale poorly with problem size or structure, reducing its utility in practice. Approaches such as the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) seek to address this by iteratively reducing an input problem until it reaches a size where it can be solved using QAOA while maintaining the same optimal solution. This algorithm, however, requires solving integer programs that have exponentially many variables, and can result in suboptimal solutions, as the integer programs may contain slack terms. In this work, we propose a heuristic called the Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) algorithm. Its novelty lies in its use of QAOA as a subroutine for sparsifying a graph through local vertex-merging. The algorithm, when used to sparsify MaxCut problems that are then solved using QAOA, achieves higher approximation ratios across all tested graphs than GDOA for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs. We then compare the time-to-solution and approximation ratio of QEGD to other QAOA variants a collection of Erdös-Rényi graphs. QEGD has higher approximation ratios on average than QAOA$^2$ and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs. It also results in higher average approximation ratios than DC-QAOA on sparse Erdös-Rényi graphs and comparable average approximation ratio on denser Erdös-Rényi graphs. However, its average wall-clock time is between 0.4\% and 5\% of the average DC-QAOA wall-clock time.

item.title: Quantum-Enhanced QSAR for DYRK1A: Evaluating Complementary and Utility QPU-Derived Molecular Representations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a quantum‑processor‑derived molecular embedding can rank drug candidates differently from traditional descriptor tables, meaning the two approaches would send distinct compound series to experimental testing. While it does not claim a formal quantum speedup, the result adds concrete evidence that QPU‑generated features may capture complementary chemical information—a theme echoed in recent quantum machine‑learning studies on small‑molecule datasets. For drug‑discovery pipelines, even modest diversification of hits could translate into new chemotypes, though larger benchmarks will be needed to confirm whether the quantum advantage is reproducible and scalable.

In drug discovery, hit identification selects a limited set of compounds for experimental evaluation from a larger collection of candidates. Because laboratory screening capacity is limited, that choice determines which chemical series continue into further investigation. A hit that is not assayed does not enter confirmation or the analog series, and that chemical series is not opened. For the DYRK1A kinase, the same test molecules were scored from a tabular representation of molecular descriptors and from a vector measured on a quantum processor, with the same RBF-SVM. The question is whether the two models propose the same set for experimental evaluation: they propose different compounds. The model on the vector measured on the quantum processor includes compounds that the tabular representation leaves out, and among them are already-labeled actives. The tabular representation includes actives that the vector measured on the quantum processor leaves out. What is reported is that set: who enters, with what label, and whether published chemistry already mentions it. No formal quantum advantage is claimed, nor a mechanism for why the two vectors separate differently. Those compounds fall within the neighborhood that both representations already cover; what changes is which model marks them active. From that follows the cost of predictive disagreement: each model would send a different chemical series to experimental evaluation.

item.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first rigorous semantic framework for reasoning about confidentiality in quantum software, extending classical noninterference concepts to handle superposition and entanglement while proving its equivalence to an attacker‑centric simulation view. By introducing “self‑conjugation,” a clever workaround to the no‑cloning obstacle, the authors enable quantum Hoare‑logic proofs of information‑flow security for protocols such as the quantum one‑time pad, error‑correcting codes and anonymous entanglement generation. The work lays essential groundwork for future toolchains that can certify secure quantum programs on cloud platforms, even though practical verification tools are still in early development.

Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

item.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides the first systematic, cloud‑based comparison of how well today’s superconducting and trapped‑ion processors can generate large GHZ states, a key resource for many quantum algorithms and error‑correction schemes. By measuring raw fidelities without mitigation, it shows that even on machines boasting dozens of physical qubits, usable multipartite entanglement often tops out at only a few dozen—while a 12‑qubit ion trap can reliably harness its full register, underscoring the current strength of connectivity and coherence in trapped‑ion platforms. The results give developers a realistic yardstick for choosing cloud providers and highlight where hardware and compilation improvements are most needed to close the gap between qubit count and functional quantum volume.

Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

item.title: Dynamical GKP codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article lifts the dynamical‑code framework from qubits to continuous‑variable GKP encodings, showing how sequences of translation measurements can protect oscillator‑based quantum information in real time. By introducing subsystem GKP codes and a Floquet square‑hexagonal construction, it achieves lower‑weight stabilizer checks while retaining the full single‑qubit Clifford set—an attractive combination for hardware platforms that already generate GKP states. The result could streamline fault‑tolerant designs for superconducting or trapped‑ion resonators, though implementing the required time‑dependent measurements with sufficient precision remains an experimental hurdle.

Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

item.title: CV-TF-QKD
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the celebrated twin‑field (TF) advantage—key rates scaling as the square root of channel loss—can be transferred to continuous‑variable (CV) QKD by using Gaussian‑modulated coherent states and an untrusted single‑photon relay. By proving composable security against general coherent attacks and delivering finite‑key rate estimates that beat both pure‑loss and thermal‑loss repeaterless bounds, the work bridges the gap between discrete‑variable TF‑QKD’s long‑distance promise and CV systems’ practical hardware compatibility. If experimental implementations can meet the modest phase‑stability and detector‑efficiency requirements outlined, CV‑TF‑QKD could become a near‑term pathway to high‑rate secure links over metropolitan and intercity fiber networks.

We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrtη$, where $η$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.

item.title: Pool-free, residual-triggered ansatz growth for variational imaginary-time evolution: when a fixed operator order beats adaptive screening
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a pool‑free, residual‑triggered growth strategy for variational imaginary‑time evolution can outperform the popular ADAPT‑VQE and AVQITE approaches on non‑integrable spin chains and stretched H₄ by cutting required circuit depth by up to a factor of five. By fixing the operator order through nested Hamiltonian commutators and only adding layers when the McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold, the method sidesteps the expensive screening and full re‑optimization steps that dominate adaptive algorithms. The result suggests a practical route to more resource‑efficient near‑term simulations of strongly correlated systems, though the advantage fades for integrable models or ultra‑high‑precision targets.

Adaptive variational algorithms such as ADAPT-VQE and AVQITE screen an operator pool at every growth step, and ADAPT-VQE also re-optimizes all parameters. We study a pool-free alternative for variational imaginary-time evolution (VITE). The layers are fixed in advance by nested commutators of the Hamiltonian, grouped by symmetry and particle number, and the next layer is appended when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold. On five non-integrable systems (the mixed-field Ising chain and tori, and stretched H$_4$), this dynamic VITE reaches a relative error of $10^{-4}$ with 1.6-5.4 times fewer circuits than the cheapest of six to eight adaptive variants, including single-Pauli-string and qubit-excitation pools and batched ADAPT-VQE. On the chain the advantage persists from 8 to 16 sites. Screening and re-optimization account for most of the adaptive methods' cost. On the spin models, a longitudinal-field scan shows that the advantage requires broken integrability, which makes adaptive screening expensive. The advantage is lost on transverse-field Ising models, at tight targets (relative error $10^{-6}$) and where the schedule front-loads weak layers.

item.title: Quantum propagation of vibrational excitation in harmonically confined trapped-ion crystal
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first experimental observation of a single‑phonon wavepacket propagating through a harmonically confined, ten‑ion crystal, showing that even modest ion chains can emulate the dynamics of mobile bosonic particles. By quantifying how the intrinsic spacing inhomogeneity shapes hopping and collective drift, the work provides practical guidance for scaling trapped‑ion simulators toward larger many‑body phonon lattices—a key step echoed in recent efforts to build phononic quantum networks and analog quantum simulators. The close match between experiment and numerics also validates the theoretical tools needed to design more complex quasiparticle simulations on existing hardware.

Vibrational excitations, or phonons, in trapped ions serve as useful resources for quantum information processing, including quantum simulation and computing. Localized excitations of ions' vibrational motion (local phonons) can be used for simulating quantum particles that propagate over a system. Here, we experimentally investigate the propagation of a localized vibrational excitation in a one-dimensional trapped-ion crystal. A 10-ion crystal confined in a harmonic potential is used. It is found that inhomogeneity in the spacing between the ions leads to characteristic behaviors such as adjacent hopping and global movement. A comparison of the experimental results with numerical simulations shows agreement up to fine details. The system explored here may be extended to many-body systems of bosonic particles as well as more complex quasiparticles.

item.title: Correlations carried and controlled by coupled non-Markovian environments
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a numerically exact “local hierarchy of pure states” method that can capture both memory effects and spatial correlations in non‑Markovian environments—a capability that has been missing from most open‑system tools until now. By showing how photon hopping between cavity modes can ferry quantum information and generate entanglement across otherwise isolated spins, the work links recent advances in cavity‑QED platforms and feedback‑based control to practical routes for engineering long‑range correlations in quantum simulators and sensors. The approach also dovetails with tensor‑network techniques, suggesting a scalable way to explore many‑body dynamics where coherent environmental transport plays a decisive role.

An environment can retain quantum information and carry it between spatially separated systems. Describing the combined influence of these processes requires a treatment of both environmental memory and spatial correlations. Here, we formulate a local hierarchy of pure states for quantum systems coupled to spatially correlated, non-Markovian environments whose modes themselves exchange excitations. We use this method to describe the reduced spin dynamics of a chain of locally coupled Rabi spin--cavity pairs motivated by cavity-QED implementations, where photon hopping in the eliminated cavity environment generates correlations and entanglement between otherwise isolated spins. Monitoring intermediate cavities and feeding their measurement records back onto the corresponding spins further enhances correlations between endpoint spins that receive no direct feedback. The delayed response when feedback starts, and continued entanglement growth after it stops, support a mechanism in which coherent environmental dynamics carry the effects of earlier feedback to the endpoint spins. Finally, tensor-network simulations of XXZ and Heisenberg chains show how environmental transport changes many-body correlation patterns. These results show how coupled environments and local feedback can control correlations between distant spins. We provide a numerically exact stochastic pure-state framework for simulating these processes, opening up avenues to explore the coherent and dissipative control of interacting non-Markovian many-body systems.

item.title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a single contextual‑bandit controller can learn on the fly which error‑mitigation tool—ZNE, PEC, measurement correction, dynamical decoupling or circuit re‑optimisation—is optimal for each step of a quantum‑machine‑learning run, delivering performance within 95 % of an oracle that knows the best choice in advance. By turning mitigation into an adaptive policy rather than a static preset, APGEM directly tackles the drift in both noise and circuit parameters that has limited variational algorithms on today’s noisy devices, and it does so without requiring any algorithm‑specific redesign. The result is a practical, hardware‑agnostic layer that could make QML experiments more reliable on near‑term processors, though the added classical decision overhead and the need for sufficient feedback signals remain important considerations.

Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

item.title: Coherent Optical Readout of Neutral-Atom Qubits via Homodyne Detection of Resonant Fluorescence
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that balanced homodyne detection of resonant fluorescence can read out neutral‑atom qubits with >99 % fidelity in under 100 µs, dramatically cutting the latency that camera‑based imaging imposes on current platforms. By analytically and numerically accounting for atomic motion and photon recoil, the authors identify an optimal detection window that preserves coherence while accumulating enough signal—a key step toward mid‑circuit measurements and fault‑tolerant error correction in neutral‑atom processors such as those from QuEra and Pasqal. The work bridges a gap between high‑speed optical readout techniques used in trapped‑ion systems and the scalability advantages of neutral atoms, though practical implementation will still need careful control of motional heating to realize the predicted performance.

Fast, non-destructive qubit readout is essential for repeated sampling, mid-circuit measurement, and fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum processing, but camera-based fluorescence detection introduces electronic latency beyond fluorescence-collection time. We propose coherent readout of the state-dependent resonant fluorescence using balanced homodyne detection with photodiodes. An analytic model quantifies the effect of atomic motion on the time-integrated quadrature signal and noise, showing that harmonic motion causes phase averaging while photon recoils produce trajectory-dependent signal fluctuations; the competition between signal accumulation and motion-induced decoherence sets an optimal detection time. Three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations validate the model and predict state-detection fidelities exceeding 99% within 100 $μ\mathrm{s}$ for experimentally realistic parameters. These results establish the readout conditions and physical constraints for rapid coherent fluorescence readout of neutral-atom qubits.

item.title: Analog quantum approximate optimization algorithm for solving the weighted MaxCut problem on three-dimensional single-atom Rydberg array
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a fully analog version of QAOA on a three‑dimensional Rydberg‑atom array that directly encodes weighted MaxCut instances in the geometry‑dependent interaction strengths, showing how hardware layout can become part of the algorithmic encoding. By pairing discretized quantum annealing with a graph‑neural‑network warm start, the authors achieve solution qualities that surpass the classic Goemans‑Williamson rounding on most test graphs and evaluate realistic pulse‑time costs under an Aquila‑style error model. The work bridges recent advances in neutral‑atom processors and machine‑learning‑guided quantum optimization, suggesting a practical pathway toward near‑term advantage for combinatorial problems on scalable analog hardware.

We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.
